name: CK-12
line: CK-12 pairs math textbooks with an AI chat tutor. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs CK-12: CK-12 pairs digital math textbooks with an AI chat tutor. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: CK-12's math is a set of digital textbooks, with Flexi, an AI tutor a student asks in a chat box, beside them [1][2]. The learner or teacher picks the book and the lesson [3]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In CK-12 the unit is the book. Its math comes as FlexBooks, digital textbooks whose lessons mix text, video, audio and quizzes [2][3]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [9].

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. In CK-12 the learner or teacher picks the book and the lesson, and Common Sense Media notes that younger children may need a parent's help to find their material [3]. CK-12 also offers adaptive practice. We found no published rule for how it picks items [2].

reasons.title: Help gives the first step
reasons.body: In AMP a hint gives the first step and never the answer. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. CK-12's tutor, Flexi, is a chat box a student types questions into [1]. In CK-12's own study of Flexi, teachers raised concerns about students relying on it too much [5]. In a field experiment with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey, which did not test Flexi, unrestricted GPT-4 raised practice scores by 48%. Once access was removed, those students scored 17% lower on exams than students who never had AI. A tutor version with learning safeguards largely mitigated that harm [6].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, on one map of skills from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. CK-12's math is a set of separate books: grades 1 to 5 as one set, a middle school book for grades 6 to 8, then one for each course from algebra up [2].

rows.range: FlexBooks from grade 1 through calculus, plus college algebra and college precalculus [2].
rows.start: CK-12 says its AI can judge in 2 to 4 questions whether a student is at, below or above grade on a concept. No accuracy figure is given [4].
rows.teaching: Digital textbooks with text, video, audio and quizzes [3], and Flexi, an AI tutor a student asks in a chat box [1][2].
rows.next: The learner or teacher picks the book and the lesson [3]. Adaptive practice exists; we found no published rule for how it picks items [2].
rows.mastery: None found in the pages we read [2][4].
rows.review: None found in the pages we read [2][3][4].
rows.adult: A teacher assigns work with a class code [1]. Common Sense Media says younger children may need a parent's help to find their material [3].
rows.reports: Insights, a feature that helps teachers read student performance [4]. Links with Google Classroom, Canvas and Schoology [2].
rows.evidence: We found no math entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [7][8]. CK-12's own studies report teachers' views and platform statistics [4][5].

theirs: CK-12 comes from the CK-12 Foundation, a nonprofit [2]. Its math is a set of FlexBooks, digital textbooks from grade 1 through algebra, geometry, trigonometry, precalculus and calculus, with college algebra and college precalculus above them [2]. The same site covers science and other subjects [2].

A FlexBook lesson mixes text, video, audio and quizzes [3], and the site also lists interactive science simulations and PLIX interactive items [2]. Beside the books sits Flexi, an AI tutor a student asks in a chat box, on the web, in a Google Play app or on WhatsApp [1][2]. The learner or teacher picks the book and the lesson [3], and teachers assign work with a class code [1].
credit: One place for math from grade 1 through calculus, in text, video, audio and quizzes [2][3].
Flexi answers the questions a learner asks in their own words [1][2].
Interactive science simulations and items beside the reading [2].

theirs: CK-12's efficacy page lists its studies [4]. The fullest is a six-week study of Flexi in spring 2025, run by CK-12 with Leanlab Education: ten middle and high school math and science teachers in five states, studied through surveys, diaries and focus groups [5]. It reports what teachers saw, with no test scores. Teachers reported more engagement, confidence and curiosity. They also reported that students struggled with prompting, and worries about overreliance and plagiarism [5].

The other entries are small studies, such as a blind rating of Flexi against Khanmigo by 25 students and a five-day pre-test and post-test with 76 students in grades 7 and 8 who used Flexi to study. The page lists no results for the rating and no scores or effect sizes for the test [4]. It also gives platform statistics, such as two in three students improving their skill level, with no sample size, comparison group or definition [4].

We found no CK-12 math study with a comparison group and published test results. Evidence for ESSA has no math entry for CK-12; its one CK-12 page, filed under science, reads "No studies met inclusion requirements" [7]. The What Works Clearinghouse has no intervention report on CK-12 [8].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [9]. In a field experiment with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey, students given unrestricted GPT-4 scored 17% lower on exams, once access was removed, than students who never had AI. A tutor version with learning safeguards largely mitigated that harm [6]. AMP gives a worked example at every problem, and no AI model runs while a learner works.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want a textbook to read and a tutor that answers your child's own questions.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want the program, not your child, to choose the next problem.
You want help that gives the first step and never the answer.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.

questions.question: How is AMP different from CK-12?
questions.answer: CK-12 pairs digital math textbooks with Flexi, an AI chat tutor, and the learner or teacher picks the lesson [1][2][3]. In AMP every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does CK-12 work?
questions.answer: We found no CK-12 math study with a comparison group and published test results, on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [4][7][8]. Its fullest study reports what ten teachers saw of Flexi, with no test scores [5].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
